common_name: Golden Drop Gooseberry (Historic Sweet Yellow Dessert Gooseberry)

planting.note: Plant dormant bushes from autumn to early spring in a cool-summer site; Golden Drop is an old English dessert type grown for eating fresh rather than cooking, so a spot with afternoon shade helps keep fruit from scalding in hot climates.

directions: Plant dormant bushes in rich, well-drained soil in a cool spot with afternoon shade, mulching to keep roots cool through summer. Golden Drop is a long-grown English dessert gooseberry prized for small-to-medium berries that ripen to an amber-yellow and carry an intensely sweet, honeyed flavor rare among gooseberries, making it a favorite for eating straight off the bush rather than cooking. The compact, upright bush is somewhat less vigorous and spreading than many culinary gooseberry types, so it fits smaller garden corners well. Prune out the oldest third of the wood each winter to keep air moving through the canopy and reduce mildew pressure on the thin-skinned fruit.

common_name: London Gooseberry (Classic Heavy-Cropping Red Dessert Gooseberry)

planting.note: Plant dormant bushes from autumn to early spring; London is an old, mildew-prone English cultivar that benefits from an open planting site with good air circulation and a preventive fungicide program in humid regions.

directions: Plant dormant bushes into fertile, well-drained soil with room for good airflow, since this cultivar is more susceptible to powdery mildew than many modern gooseberries and needs an open site to stay healthy. London is one of the oldest named gooseberry cultivars still grown, historically prized among English gooseberry clubs for producing some of the largest berries of any traditional variety, ripening to a deep red with a rich, sweet flavor once fully colored. The vigorous, spreading bush crops heavily and dependably once established. Prune to an open, uncrowded framework each winter and watch closely for mildew through the growing season, treating early if it appears.
sources: RV Roger Ltd soft fruit nursery

common_name: Rondom Red Currant (Late-Season High-Sugar Dutch Red Currant)

planting.note: Plant dormant bushes in fall or early spring; Rondom flowers and ripens later than most red currants, which lets it dodge late spring frosts and extends the harvest after earlier cultivars have finished.

directions: Plant dormant bushes in fertile, well-drained, cool soil in partial shade to full sun, mulching to keep roots cool through summer heat. Rondom is a Dutch-bred red currant valued for flowering and ripening later than most other cultivars, which both helps the blossoms escape late frosts and stretches the home garden's currant harvest into a second wave after earlier varieties are done. Its long, well-filled trusses of firm, pale red berries carry an unusually high sugar content for a red currant, giving a milder, less tart eating experience than classic types. Because fruit forms on spurs of older wood, prune to an open vase shape in winter and remove canes older than three years to keep the bush productive.

common_name: Rolan Red Currant (Vigorous Self-Fertile Mid-Season Red Currant)

planting.note: Plant dormant bushes in fall or early spring into fertile, moisture-retentive soil; Rolan is self-fertile and needs no second currant nearby to crop well.

directions: Plant dormant bushes in fertile, well-drained soil enriched with organic matter, in partial shade to full sun, and keep roots mulched through summer. Rolan is a vigorous, upright red currant that sets heavy mid-season crops of glossy, translucent bright red berries on long, well-formed clusters, with good resistance to the common fungal leaf diseases that trouble many currant plantings. Because it is reliably self-fertile, a single bush fruits well without a pollinator partner, making it a practical choice for small gardens with room for only one currant. Prune in the dormant season to an open framework and remove the oldest wood each year, since the best fruit comes from one- to three-year-old stems.

common_name: Big Ben Black Currant (Extra-Large-Fruited Early Scottish Cultivar)

planting.note: Plant dormant bushes from autumn through early spring, setting the crown slightly deeper than it grew in the nursery to encourage vigorous basal shoots; Big Ben ripens earlier than most other Ben-series currants.

directions: Plant dormant bushes in fertile, moisture-retentive soil in partial shade to full sun, burying the crown a little deeper than in the pot to promote strong new growth from the base. Released in 2013 as the newest addition to the Scottish Ben series of black currants bred at the James Hutton Institute, Big Ben stands out for berries noticeably larger than older cultivars in the series, with a sweeter, higher-sugar flavor that holds up well for fresh eating as well as cooking. It crops heavily and early in the season, and shows good resistance to mildew and leaf spot compared with many older black currant varieties. Prune in the dormant season by removing roughly a quarter of the oldest wood annually, since the heaviest fruiting happens on one- and two-year-old stems.
sources: James Hutton Institute — Soft Fruit Breeding

common_name: White Soul Alpine Strawberry (Bird-Resistant Everbearing White Woodland Strawberry)

planting.note: Start White Soul's tiny seed indoors on the soil surface under light several weeks before the last frost, then transplant the compact clumps out into rich, moisture-retentive soil once frost danger has passed.

directions: Start White Soul's dust-fine seed indoors on the soil surface under light, since steady moisture and light exposure are both needed for germination, then transplant into rich, well-drained soil in partial shade after the last frost. Unlike the common red-fruited alpine strawberries, this selection ripens to a creamy white-to-pale-yellow color that birds tend to pass over, letting more of the small, intensely aromatic berries reach the gardener. Plants stay compact and send out no runners, so they hold a tidy clump shape well suited to shaded edging, containers, or tucking beneath taller shade-loving shrubs. Harvest continues from late spring into fall, and dividing congested clumps every few years keeps plants productive.
